papers.title: When Agentic Retrieval Fails Silently: Framework and Production Evidence from a Creative AI Assistant
papers.authors: Yan, Liang, Anuj Agarwal, Aditya Reddy Cheruku
papers.abstract: CTR, MRR, and behavioral NDCG assume the user sees ranked results and acts on them. In an agentic assistant, a generation layer consumes retrieval output first, and that assumption breaks in three ways. The agent reads the results before the user does (who). The user's action can come several turns or sessions after retrieval (when). Outcomes blend retrieved content with the model's own knowledge (what caused it). We call this the attribution gap. We propose Layered Agentic Retrieval Assessment (LARA), which measures retrieval quality, engagement and outcome, and product success as three independent layers joined by a four-field lineage schema that requires no new modeling. We examine the motivation on Adobe Express, where one retrieval infrastructure serves a gallery search surface and an agentic assistant at roughly one-eighth its session volume for the same user population. Chat users reformulate more than gallery users (44.4% vs. 33.1%) because chat reformulation refines generated output. LARA restores attribution for the retrieval.

deep_reading.title: When Agentic Retrieval Fails Silently: Framework and Production Evidence from a Creative AI Assistant
deep_reading.content:
On Adobe Express, one retrieval infrastructure serves both a template gallery search and an agentic assistant, for the same user population. Intuition says assistant users, who never inspect result lists, should reformulate less; in fact the chat entry point reformulates 44.4% of the time against 33.1% in the gallery, 11 points higher. The two "reformulations" are different behaviors: in the gallery it means "these results were not relevant, I will try another query"; in chat it mostly means "I see the generated output and want to change it" ("make it bluer", "try a bolder font"). More surprising still, ==the assistant actually fired retrieval on only 0.31% of prompts==. The three Adobe authors call this the **attribution gap**: CTR, MRR and behavioral NDCG assume the user sees ranked results and acts on them, and in an agentic assistant that assumption fails in three directions at once. The paper proposes LARA, a layered assessment framework that restores retrieval attribution with three independent measurement layers plus four logging fields, and no new modeling.

## 1. The problem: the agent reads first, the user arrives later

The authors distil the failure into three structural shifts and stress that none is a tuning problem.

**Who reads.** In gallery search a user types "birthday invitation", scans 40 templates and clicks one, and that click grades retrieval. In the assistant, the user asks for a birthday invitation, the search subagent retrieves templates, and the agent picks one and builds the design; the user never sees the other 39. There may be no click at all, and whatever the user does see has already been filtered and reordered by the agent.

**When the user acts.** In one conversation the same asset can be retrieved in turn 1 and again in turn 3, then exported in turn 5 or in another session. Without an identifier linking the action to a specific retrieval event, timing cannot say which retrieval earned it.

**What caused it.** A bad outcome cannot be split into retrieval failure versus generation failure, and a good outcome can hide a retrieval failure the model quietly compensated for.

![Paper Table 1: the assumption each structural shift breaks, how today's metrics mislead, and the LARA fix.](figs/2610.30423/crop_tab1.png)

Without per-component instrumentation, teams rely on session-level proxies such as retry, abandonment and task completion. The authors note that retry alone fails both ways: it fires on generation failures unrelated to retrieval, and stays silent when the model covers for a retrieval failure. The third shift is the most dangerous, because nothing in the session-level signal distinguishes it from success.

## 2. Method: three measurement layers

LARA measures each stage at the earliest point where its failure becomes observable.

![Paper Figure 1: LARA's three layers. Layer 1 needs only server-side logs; Layers 2 and 3 need the lineage schema on the right that spans all three.](figs/2610.30423/crop_fig1.png)

**Layer 1: retrieval quality.** Did the subagent return the right assets in the right order? Metrics are null rate, precision@1, precision@K and NDCG@K, computed from server-side logs against offline relevance labels (human or LLM-as-judge) at the moment retrieval fires, independent of what the user or agent does next. CTR becomes a secondary directional signal. Only this layer can detect a silent retrieval failure the model compensated for.

**Layer 2: engagement and outcome.** Did anyone use what retrieval returned, and did anything signal that retrieval was wrong? This layer keeps positive and failure evidence separate and reports both by "retrieval role", a tag written at retrieval time recording what retrieval was for: direct retrieval, retrieve-then-inspect, retrieve-then-act, reference input for generation, an embedded step in a larger task, or context-dependent. Its four metrics are:

- **Genuine Positive Rate (GPR)**: the share of retrievals followed by user-initiated use of a returned asset after the response is shown, such as a follow-up prompt that continues with it, or selecting, editing or exporting it.
- **Agent Consumption Rate (ACR)**: the share of retrievals where the agent uses a returned asset within the same request, before the user has a result (e.g., finding a logo and removing its background in one prompt). It is positive evidence too, but tracked separately, because the agent using an asset is the agent's judgment while a user's later action is independent confirmation.
- **Observed Retrieval Failure Rate (ORF)**: the share of retrievals followed by one of three retrieval-specific signals: Search Correction (the user says the retrieved object or route was wrong), Search Reformulation (retrying retrieval for the same unresolved need), or Agentic Rejection (the workflow was expected to use a returned asset but used something else). A Downstream Correction that keeps the asset and fixes an edit or generation is not a retrieval failure. 1−ORF is reported alongside GPR and ACR but never read as satisfaction.
- **Unobserved Outcome Rate (UOR)**: the share of retrievals with neither use evidence nor a failure signal, reported as its own category, not as abandonment or success.

**Layer 3: product success.** Did the user achieve the goal? In creative tools the clearest signals are export, share and download. Task completion is defined per retrieval role, and goal fulfillment needs LLM-as-judge or human annotation. This layer becomes a retrieval signal, not just a product-health signal, only when the success event links back through the lineage fields to the retrieval that supplied the asset.

## 3. Cross-layer diagnosis and lineage fields

Reading Layer 1 against Layer 2 locates the failing stage:

| Layer 1 | Layer 2 | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | ORF high | Retrieval returned the wrong assets |
| High | ORF low, many Downstream Corrections | Assets fine, generation failed |
| High | ORF high (Agentic Rejection) | Agent bypassed good results (parametric blending) |
| Low | ORF near zero | Silent retrieval failure masked by the model |

The last row is the most dangerous: invisible without Layer 1, and detectable with it at fire time, before complaints accumulate.

**Four lineage fields.** In current production logs, retrieval events and action events share no field. The authors close the gap with four: a unique `retrieval_id` on every retrieval event; `returned_asset_ids`, the full ranked list at fire time, before the generation layer filters or reorders it, which alone enables Layer 1 and is the highest-value single change; `consumed_asset_id` on every action event, whether a user action or an agent tool call; and `source_retrieval_id` on the same event, naming the retrieval that supplied the asset, inherited from the placement event for assets already in the document. All four are logging additions, not predictive models. Because `source_retrieval_id` names a retrieval rather than a session, it resolves cross-turn recurrence and keeps exports in a new session attributable; joined, the fields recover the retrieval rank of the asset actually used, independent of display order, letting RAG frameworks such as RAGAs and ARES use direct attribution instead of timing heuristics.

**Illustration**: a user in chat says "find a birthday invitation template and change the title to Xiaoming's 6th birthday". The retrieval event logs `retrieval_id=r1` and 20 candidates; the agent picks rank 4 and edits the title, an agent event carrying `consumed_asset_id` and `source_retrieval_id=r1`, which counts toward ACR; two days later the user exports in the editor, and the export inherits r1, counting as a retrieval-attributed export in Layer 3. Without these fields, the export lands in another session and the chat session is scored as abandoned.

## 4. Production evidence from Adobe Express

The authors analysed production sessions from August 2026. LARA's lineage fields are not yet implemented, so every engagement figure below is timing-based; session, user and query counts are withheld under Adobe's disclosure policy, and the gallery runs at about 8–9× the assistant's volume.

![Paper Table 3: legacy behavioral proxies for gallery search vs the agentic assistant on Adobe Express, August 2026, same retrieval infrastructure and users.](figs/2610.30423/crop_tab3.png)

**The agent reads first.** Assistant-wide CTR is near zero because 99.7% of interactions never invoke retrieval, so no denominator exists. Retrieval fired on only 0.31% of in-scope prompts; where it fires it works, with a 1.51% null rate and about 1.05 clicks per returned grid. The direct test needs ACR, which cannot yet be computed.

**Action is delayed.** Assistant sessions average 2.04 prompts (chat: 2.65), so the same asset reappears in later turns. Exports started from chat land in a different `session_guid` once the user leaves the chat surface; session-level attribution counts these users as abandoning, inflating chat abandonment (59.5%) and deflating engagement.

**Retrieval and generation blend.** This is the reformulation reversal from the opening: one behavioral signal mixes retrieval failure with generation refinement, and the aggregate means nothing on its own. LARA splits it into Search Reformulation, counted only on retrieval turns, and Downstream Correction, counted everywhere else.

**What can be measured today.** Null rate and clicks per grid come from existing logs; precision@K and NDCG@K need `returned_asset_ids` plus a labeled sample; GPR, ACR, ORF and UOR need the other three fields and the retrieval role, and today require manual trace annotation. The team can confirm retrieval works when it fires, but not yet whether the user or agent used what it returned.

## 5. Unexpected finding: retrieval nearly vanishes

Gallery search is retrieval by definition, while the assistant invoked retrieval on 0.31% of prompts, and about 82% of assistant activity is generative editing with no gallery-search analog. The authors suspect the bigger risk is **missed retrieval**: the planner routes "find me a birthday invitation template" to generative editing, no retrieval event fires, and Layer 1 has nothing to score. Table 3's 10.7% chat retrieval-intent figure is directional; if it reflects intent rather than fired retrieval, its gap to 0.31% is a first estimate of missed retrieval. They name this Layer 0 (planner routing), an extension of LARA rather than a fourth layer, with two measures: mis-routing rate (retrieval calls whose prompt is out of retrieval scope, to be excluded from Layer 1) and missed-retrieval rate (prompts with retrieval intent that never triggered retrieval, which needs ground-truth intent labels). In a 273-prompt sample, roughly 5–7% contained two or more distinct retrieval intents.

## 6. Limitations and industry relevance

The authors' limitations are concrete: all evidence comes from one deployment, and the 0.31% rate and the reformulation reversal may be specific to creative assistants dominated by generative editing; none of the lineage fields is implemented, so all Layer 2 figures are timing-based inferences and retrieval role is inferred post hoc rather than tagged at retrieval time; chat abandonment is overstated by cross-session exports; the data has not passed schema or value-range validation, synthetic traffic was removed manually, and latency and tokens per successful task are not instrumented per stage. LARA starts at the retrieval component; how the agent interprets intent, generates queries or decomposes multi-intent requests needs separate instrumentation. It is a short industry paper, and the framework has not been validated across deployments or by online experiments.

The authors' three lessons for practitioners are practical. First, ==do not report assistant-wide CTR or reformulation as retrieval metrics==; restrict retrieval metrics to turns where retrieval fired and split reformulation into Search Reformulation and Downstream Correction. Second, log the full ranked list at fire time before anything else; it is the only field that unblocks Layer 1. Third, define user-initiated use once and publish the definition: Express chat's meaningful-action rate moved between 7.6% and 40.5% depending on which actions qualified. For teams embedding search into agents, the main value is the reminder that when retrieval fires on 0.31% of prompts, the question is not only whether it ranked well but whether it was called at all.

papers.title: AutoSim: A Self-Improving User Simulator for Conversational Search Evaluation
papers.authors: Saber Zerhoudi, Jelena Mitrovic, Michael Granitzer
papers.abstract: User simulators promise to evaluate conversational search systems at a scale human studies cannot reach, but only if their behavior is realistic enough to trust. We study AutoSim, a conversational-search user simulator whose relevance judgments rank a controlled pool of retrieval systems in agreement with NIST across three TREC iKAT years (Kendall's $τ$ of $0.66$, $0.91$, and $0.91$; all $p{\le}0.002$), an agreement that survives removing its persona. AutoSim self-improves against a held-out signal from real users, and we find that fine-tuning its weights makes it behave like real users, which in turn gives a more accurate estimate of how well a system serves them. Reaching that behavior takes more than prompting: when discriminating between real and simulated user sessions, no prompt we tried lowers a held-out real-versus-simulated classifier below AUC $0.85$, whereas fine-tuning the weights drives it to $0.45$, where neither the classifier nor a human reading full dialogues can tell it from a real user. That added realism is what makes the evaluation more accurate: where real users retrieve little, a prompted simulator over-estimates retrieval effectiveness by $+0.136$ nDCG and returns a relevant passage on $57\%$ of the turns where real users find none, enough to change a deployment decision. Only the weight-level simulator escapes this bias. We release the framework and code.
papers.summary: Conversational search needs trustworthy user simulators for scale. AutoSim’s relevance judgments rank a controlled pool of retrieval systems in agreement with NIST across three TREC iKAT years (Kendall τ 0.66 / 0.91 / 0.91, all p≤0.002), and that agreement survives removing its persona. Self-improving against held-out real-user signal, weight-level self-improvement drives real-vs-sim AUC from ~0.85 down to 0.45, lifts retrieval +0.136 nDCG, and returns a relevant passage on 57% of turns. ==A simulator is trustworthy when it ranks systems like NIST, not when it merely sounds human==.

deep_reading.title: AutoSim: A Self-Improving User Simulator for Conversational Search Evaluation
deep_reading.content:
Ask a strong LLM to play a search user and it writes 37.5 words per message where real users write 12.8; a held-out discriminator catches its utterances at AUC 0.88, and its queries retrieve almost none of the passages a real user retrieves (overlap@5 of 0.01). This SIGIR-AP 2026 paper studies AutoSim, a conversational-search user simulator whose relevance judgments rank retrieval systems in agreement with NIST across three TREC iKAT years (Kendall's τ of 0.66, 0.91, 0.91), yet whose user behavior is far from human. The authors let the simulator self-improve under a held-out signal from real users, and the conclusion is clear: ==editing the prompt cannot push discriminator AUC below 0.85; editing the weights drives it to 0.45==, where even a person reading the full dialogue cannot tell. More importantly, that realism changes the evaluation: where real users retrieve poorly, a prompted simulator over-estimates nDCG by 0.136, enough to change a deployment decision.

![Real-vs-simulated discriminator AUC on held-out iKAT for four simulator configurations: default prompt, tuned prompt, few-shot prompting, and a weight-level fine-tune (AutoSim); 0.5 means indistinguishable.](figs/2610.28054/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: can simulators be trusted, and what should be edited to make them human

User simulation lets conversational-search systems be compared reproducibly, when tuning a ranker or a clarifying-question policy, without a human study for every design change. But a simulator is fixed at design time as personas, prompts and rules, and does not change as the systems it evaluates do. Prior work also finds it an unreliable proxy: changing only the underlying user model swings the evaluated agent's task success by about nine percentage points, and general-purpose LLM simulators systematically over-estimate success. Nor is a more realistic simulator necessarily a more accurate evaluator.

The authors split the question into three: does AutoSim rank IR systems as NIST does (RQ1); can self-improvement close the behavioral gap to real users, and should it edit the prompt or the weights (RQ2); and does closing the gap make the simulator a better evaluator (RQ3)? The diagnosis in Section 3 sets the direction: the default simulator's relevance judging already agrees with NIST, the gap is in "what the user says and asks for", and editing the generation prompt does not close it. So the design leaves the relevance judge alone, targets the utterance generator, and edits it at the weights.

## 2. Method: AutoSim and the self-improvement loop

![AutoSim drives a real conversational-search system: the loop records traces and proposes edits, accepting one only if it does not regress on a held-out split; the editable components are the relevance-judging instruction and the utterance generator.](figs/2610.28054/hf2.png)

**Simulator state.** AutoSim keeps an ordinary LLM generator and wraps it in a state $S_t=\{P,I_t,H_t,C_{s,t}\}$: persona $P$ (background statements in a personal text knowledge base, PTKB), information need $I_t$, dialogue history $H_t$, and a latent cognitive-affective state $C_{s,t}$ such as satisfaction, frustration and patience. An orchestration policy picks which component acts each turn: deterministic simulators for routine behavior such as query reformulation, clicks and stopping, or LLM functions for answering a clarifying question, giving feedback, expressing satisfaction and generating the next utterance.

**Two editable components.** The first is the **relevance-judging instruction**, which sets the simulator's satisfaction and thus the ranking it induces; the second is the **utterance generator**, the model that writes what the simulated user says. The generator can be edited at the prompt or at the parameters, the central variable of the paper.

**Gap metric.** The authors combine system-ranking agreement and behavioral-distribution match into CSG. Communication style (D1) is measured two ways: summary statistics such as mean words, politeness rate and short-message rate, which are easy to read off and easy to write into a prompt; and a held-out real-versus-simulated discriminator reported as ROC AUC, where 0.5 means indistinguishable. The latter is an adversarial realism criterion that cannot be met by matching a few numbers, and the difference between the two measures is itself a result.

**The loop.** Each cycle records structured traces (each turn's policy choice, retrieval, click and utterance), clusters the differences between simulated and real behavior, builds per-cluster evaluators with a judge from a different model family than the generator, proposes edits by reflective population search, accepts an edit only if it does not regress on a calibration split, and monitors a rolling held-out set. The **weight-level** edit warm-starts Qwen2.5-3B with a LoRA adapter (r=16, α=32, on q/v projections) on real iKAT utterances, then runs 4 rounds of adversarial rejection sampling: sample several utterances per held-out turn, keep those a frozen discriminator rates most human, fine-tune on them, refresh the discriminator.

**Testbed.** iKAT 2023 (176 judged turns), 2024 (116) and the multi-session 2025 (45), all over ClueWeb22-B with NIST passage qrels. Each year has 12 constructed retrieval systems: BM25, SPLADE and RRF first stages over raw, context-resolved and PTKB-expanded queries, with or without a cross-encoder reranker; 2023 adds two real organizer runs for 14. The reference ranking uses condensed nDCG@5 on the NIST qrels, and AutoSim's ranking uses its persona-conditioned mean satisfaction with each system's top-5 passages. The validity pipeline uses two open-weight instruction models from different families (an 80B-class Qwen and a 31B-class Gemma) at temperature 0, with no proprietary API.

## 3. RQ1: it is a valid evaluator

On the 12 iKAT 2023 systems τ=0.66 (p=0.002, system-level bootstrap 95% CI [0.30, 0.90]); leave-one-out τ ranges 0.59–0.73, and five re-scorings give 0.72±0.01. With the two real organizer runs added τ=0.65, and AutoSim ranks the weak automatic-rewrite run last, as NIST does; its largest disagreement is placing the strong manual-rewrite run 10th of 14 where NIST places it 3rd.

![RQ1: across 14 systems, AutoSim's satisfaction tracks NIST condensed nDCG@5 (Kendall τ=0.65, p=0.001); orange points are the two real organizer runs.](figs/2610.28054/hf3.png)

| --- | ---: |
| None (default prompt) | 0.88 |
| Prompt-level (best of four methods) | 0.84 |

| Query source | Words | iKAT 2024 bias | 2023 held-out bias |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Default (verbose) | 28 | +0.136 | +0.009 |
| Terse prompt | 9 | +0.087 | −0.028 |
| Length-matched truncation | 11 | +0.071 | −0.042 |
| Weight-level | 12 | +0.014 | +0.015 |

papers.title: Learning Marginal Viewpoint Utility for Budgeted Evidence Selection in RAG
papers.authors: Yiyang Duan, Ziqi Yu, Tiantong Wu, Yebo Wu, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over multi-viewpoint queries must preserve distinct answers and positions from the retrieved evidence while operating under a fixed context budget. We introduce LMVU, a lightweight ranker that learns to prioritize candidates by the marginal viewpoint coverage they add to the current selection. Training uses viewpoint annotations from each benchmark's development split to compare candidates within the same selection state. At inference, LMVU repeatedly scores budget-feasible candidates as the context grows, without accessing these annotations. We evaluate two forms of recovered viewpoint coverage: RVC$_1$ assigns each viewpoint full credit for at least one supporting source unit, while RVC$_2$ assigns half credit for one and full credit for two or more distinct source units. Exact oracles measure achievable coverage under the same evidence pool and budget. Across four viewpoint-annotated benchmarks at a 1,024-token budget, LMVU achieves gains of up to 0.047 and 0.052 points in RVC$_1$ and RVC$_2$, respectively, over the strongest non-oracle baseline for each benchmark and metric, and reaches the exact viewpoint-breadth ceiling on two benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multi-viewpoint RAG must keep distinct answers and stances under a fixed context budget. LMVU ranks by the marginal viewpoint coverage a candidate adds to the current selection, trained with viewpoint annotations that compare candidates in the same selection state, and rescoring budget-feasible candidates as context grows. It reaches 94.6% coverage on Perspectrum and matches or nears full coverage on WVS/ESS10, beating the strongest baselines. ==For multi-viewpoint retrieval, rank by marginal coverage, not per-doc relevance alone==.

deep_reading.title: Learning Marginal Viewpoint Utility for Budgeted Evidence Selection in RAG
deep_reading.content:
Ask about electoral participation and a complete answer should cover three groups: people who voted, people who did not, and people who were ineligible. A context made only of voters' responses represents one viewpoint, even if every record is accurate and relevant. Under a 1,024-token context budget, classic MMR repeatedly picks evidence supporting the same three viewpoints for a WVS corruption-perception query and leaves out "no corruption perceived". This paper from Nanyang Technological University and the University of Toronto proposes LMVU, a linear ranker with just 18 coefficients that selects evidence by how many uncovered viewpoints it adds to the current context. On four viewpoint-annotated benchmarks, ==it reaches the exact oracle's full coverage of 1.0000 on the protected WVS fold and a four-benchmark mean RVC of 0.9588, above all 16 non-oracle methods==, including two neural rerankers that cost orders of magnitude more to train.

![(a) Evidence selected for a WVS corruption-perception query from the same pool under a 1,024-token budget: MMR covers three viewpoints, LMVU adds the corruption-free perception and covers all four; (b) MMR's mean coverage gap to the exact full-pool optimum on each benchmark.](figs/2610.29234/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: relevant is not the same as covering

RAG usually ranks passages by query relevance and puts the top ones in the context. But some queries need coverage of different answers or positions, which the authors call viewpoints: an answer category or position the evidence supports. Highly relevant evidence may all support the same viewpoint and leave others unrepresented. MMR trades relevance against similarity to already-selected evidence, and recent high-diversity RAG selection follows the same idea, but semantic diversity is not viewpoint coverage: differently worded evidence can support one viewpoint, and similar wording can express opposing ones.

Formally, a query $q$ has a full candidate pool $E(q)$ and an annotated viewpoint inventory $V_q$; each item $e$ has token cost $c(e)$ and supports a viewpoint subset $V(e)$. The goal is to maximize recovered viewpoint coverage $\mathrm{RVC}(S)=|\bigcup_{e\in S}V(e)|/|V_q|$ subject to $\sum c(e)\le B$, crediting each viewpoint once. The key constraint is **label blindness**: gold viewpoint annotations are for training and evaluation only and are invisible at inference, so the selector must estimate coverage gains from observable evidence features and the current selection state. With gold access, the authors solve the full-pool optimum $S^\star_q$ exactly by viewpoint-subset dynamic programming, so they can measure how far any allocator is from optimal: its headroom.

## 2. Method: learning marginal viewpoint utility

![LMVU overview: (a) on development data, realized gold marginal gains give within-state preference pairs to train a linear scorer; (b) at runtime, label-blind, it greedily picks among budget-feasible candidates and rescores after each addition.](figs/2610.29234/hf2.png)

**Target signal.** What an allocator really needs is a candidate's marginal gain given the current selection, $\Delta V(e\mid q,S)=|V(e)\setminus V(S)|$. The same candidate's gain changes as the selection grows and drops to zero once its viewpoints are covered. $\Delta V$ needs gold labels and cannot be deployed, but it is computable on development data and can supervise a surrogate scorer $f_\theta(q,S,e)$.

**Training states.** On frozen development pools (MMR-oversampled at λ=0.5), five policies are rolled out: dense-relevance greedy, live MMR, two pinned-seed random orders, and a gold-guided marginal-gain policy. Prefix states of up to nine steps are snapshotted and deduplicated, and each state scores at most 20 candidates (dense top-10 plus a deterministic uniform draw), with gold labels giving realized gains.

**Scoring and learning.** $f_\theta=\theta^\top\tilde\phi(q,S,e)$ is linear in 18 features in four groups: candidate descriptors (4), evidence–state geometry (5), atomic–state geometry (5) and shared state descriptors (4). All similarity geometry reuses the frozen embeddings already computed for dense scoring, adding no model dependency. The static ablation M0 uses only three features: dense relevance, query–candidate cosine and candidate length. Shared state descriptors are identical for all candidates in a state, cancel in the differences and get exactly zero coefficients, so the budget acts only through the feasibility filter, not the score.

Training avoids pointwise regression because gain scales differ across states (from zero to the number of uncovered viewpoints). The authors form ordered pairs $(e^+,e^-)$ only within a state, with $\Delta V(e^+)>\Delta V(e^-)$, at most 20 per state and ties dropped; each pair yields two antisymmetric examples fit with an L2-regularized pairwise logistic (Bradley–Terry) loss, convex, by LBFGS with C=1.0. Differencing cancels state-specific additive offsets, and the pairwise loss optimizes exactly the decision the allocator faces at each step. Unlike MMR's fixed λ, LMVU's weights are fixed at inference but act on geometry features that update with the selection, so the effective novelty penalty varies with what is covered: a candidate can rank high early and drop once its viewpoint enters the selection.

**Allocation.** Starting from an empty context, each step takes the argmax only among candidates whose full cost fits the remaining budget, adds it and updates the state, and stops when nothing fits; evidence is never truncated. Each step costs $O(|F_t|\cdot18)$, maintained with incremental statistics and no pool-level similarity matrix. The authors state plainly that LMVU inherits only greedy's feasibility guarantee and has no coverage approximation bound.

## 3. Experimental setup

Four benchmarks: survey-derived WVS and ESS10, claim–perspective Perspectrum, and argument-key-point ArgKP (a saturation control). Mean full-pool sizes at budget 1024 are 507, 9, 76 and 88, and evaluation queries number 6, 97, 6 and 34. Budgets are 512, 1024 and 2048, with 1024 primary. WVS uses the protected respondent fold USA 4, which allows only predeclared evaluations and read-only audits, never fitting. The encoder is a frozen local all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Besides breadth RVC₁, the paper reports repeated support RVC₂: a viewpoint with one supporting source unit gets 0.5, and two or more distinct units get 1. Baselines are Random, BM25, FacLoc, xQuAD, SubMix, LexRank, Dense, CeRerank, Cluster, MMR and M0, plus AdaGReS, MMKP and the neural rerankers JPR and RichRAG under the same protocol. Audits confirm no runtime gold-field access across 28,314 per-query allocator runs. The authors also note that, given prior held-out inspection, this full-pool extension is exploratory rather than a fresh confirmatory test.

## 4. Main results

RVC (breadth) and RVC₂ (repeated support) at budget 1024, excerpt:

| Method | WVS | Perspectrum | ArgKP | ESS10 | Avg | RVC₂ Avg |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Dense | 0.7833 | 0.9126 | 1.0000 | 0.7306 | 0.8566 | 0.7695 |
| FacLoc | 0.9167 | 0.9108 | 1.0000 | 0.8130 | 0.9101 | 0.8469 |
| MMR | 0.9167 | 0.9296 | 1.0000 | 0.8427 | 0.9222 | 0.8314 |
| MMKP | 0.6241 | 0.9482 | 0.9667 | 0.2502 | 0.6973 | 0.5468 |
| M0 (static) | 0.7981 | 0.9495 | 0.9250 | 0.8287 | 0.8753 | 0.8065 |
| JPR | 0.8361 | 0.9074 | 1.0000 | 0.7197 | 0.8658 | 0.8233 |
| RichRAG | 0.8167 | 0.8908 | 0.9234 | 0.9569 | 0.8970 | 0.8362 |
| **LMVU** | **1.0000** | 0.9457 | **1.0000** | 0.8893 | **0.9588** | **0.8795** |
| Oracle | 1.0000 | 0.9987 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.9997 | — |

MMR's headroom to the exact oracle is 0.083, 0.069 and 0.157 on WVS, Perspectrum and ESS10, and zero on ArgKP. LMVU recovers all of it on WVS, gains 0.0466 over MMR on the headroom-richest ESS10 (30% recovered), and ties the ceiling on ArgKP. Three observations: lexical relevance alone (BM25) trails embedding methods on WVS and Perspectrum; structured diversity heuristics are benchmark-dependent, e.g. MMKP beats MMR on Perspectrum but collapses to 0.2502 on ESS10 as its per-cluster cap binds; and only the learned state-dependent utility beats MMR on all three headroom-positive benchmarks.

On significance, paired differences against MMR are nonnegative on every benchmark, but only the Perspectrum repeated-support gain (+0.0213, 95% CI [+0.007, +0.037]) has an interval excluding zero. Against other baselines, the larger folds give significance, e.g. on ESS10 +0.170 over JPR and +0.225 over AdaGReS (p<0.001). The counterexample is RichRAG overtaking LMVU on ESS10 (−0.068, p=0.004). Both neural methods win only single benchmarks: JPR reaches the ArgKP ceiling already at 512 tokens, RichRAG leads ESS10 breadth at every budget, yet both trail MMR on WVS and Perspectrum. The cost gap is huge: on one L20 GPU, JPR takes 150.5 s per fit and RichRAG (SFT+DPO) 962.7 s, plus about 11 GPU-hours of neural inference for evaluation; LMVU refits its 18 coefficients on CPU in seconds (1.3 s measured for the largest benchmark's 13,952 development states) and scores each candidate with one 18-dimensional dot product.

## 5. State conditioning, transfer and boundaries

**What state contributes.** LMVU beats static M0 by 0.202 on WVS, 0.075 on ArgKP and 0.061 on ESS10; Perspectrum is the exception, where M0 is 0.004 higher. A capacity-matched null, M1-SHUF, keeps all 18 features but shuffles the 14 state features within each state, and development ranking collapses to the static level (WVS NDCG@5 0.6002 vs LMVU's 0.7944), so the gain comes from state information, not capacity. Removing the six atomic-granularity features drops WVS development NDCG@5 from 0.6597 to 0.4418.

**Cross-benchmark transfer.** Trained leave-one-benchmark-out on the other three benchmarks' development states, the model still beats MMR on development folds by 0.150 on WVS, 0.044 on Perspectrum and 0.037 on ESS10, with full coverage on WVS, suggesting the coefficients capture a reusable coverage regularity.

**Repeated support.** Under RVC₂ the ordering mostly holds, but on WVS the relevance-free FacLoc edges ahead (0.9167 vs 0.9015). Depth holds more residual headroom: on WVS LMVU's breadth is at the full-pool optimum while depth is still 0.0985 short; ESS10 has a 0.1107 breadth gap and 0.1544 depth gap.

![Held-out RVC at each token budget (stars: exact oracle): ArgKP saturates at 1024/2048, and LMVU reaches the WVS oracle at every budget.](figs/2610.29234/hf4.png)

**Budgets and encoders.** The WVS gain over MMR is largest at 512 tokens (+0.117), +0.083 at 1024 and narrows to +0.042 at 2048, as the relaxed budget lets MMR buy the missing viewpoints; at 1024 the whole WVS gain sits in the corruption-perception issue group (+0.250). Realized gains track available headroom (Pearson r=0.574, n=4, descriptive only) and vanish where the ceiling is met. Results shift with the encoder: with bge-base, +0.025 on Perspectrum and +0.074 on ESS10 with intervals excluding zero; with bge-m3, smaller gains with intervals crossing zero, and −0.0417 on WVS.

On four viewpoint-annotated benchmarks, it reaches the exact oracle's full coverage of 1.0000 on the protected WVS fold and a four-benchmark mean RVC of 0.9588, above all 16 non-oracle methods, including two neural rerankers that cost orders of magnitude more to train.

RAG usually ranks passages by query relevance and puts the top ones in the context. But some queries need coverage of different answers or positions, which the authors call viewpoints: an answer category or position the evidence supports. Highly relevant evidence may all support the same viewpoint and leave others unrepresented. MMR trades relevance against similarity to already-selected evidence, and recent high-diversity RAG selection follows the same idea, but semantic diversity is not viewpoint coverage: differently worded evidence can support one viewpoint, and similar wording can express opposing ones.

Formally, a query q has a full candidate pool $E(q)$ and an annotated viewpoint inventory Vq​; each item e has token cost $c(e)$ and supports a viewpoint subset $V(e)$. The goal is to maximize recovered viewpoint coverage RVC(S)=∣⋃e∈S​V(e)∣/∣Vq​∣ subject to ∑c(e)≤B, crediting each viewpoint once. The key constraint is label blindness: gold viewpoint annotations are for training and evaluation only and are invisible at inference, so the selector must estimate coverage gains from observable evidence features and the current selection state. With gold access, the authors solve the full-pool optimum Sq⋆​ exactly by viewpoint-subset dynamic programming, so they can measure how far any allocator is from optimal: its headroom.

Target signal. What an allocator really needs is a candidate's marginal gain given the current selection, ΔV(e∣q,S)=∣V(e)∖V(S)∣. The same candidate's gain changes as the selection grows and drops to zero once its viewpoints are covered. ΔV needs gold labels and cannot be deployed, but it is computable on development data and can supervise a surrogate scorer fθ​(q,S,e).

Training states. All similarity geometry reuses the frozen embeddings already computed for dense scoring, adding no model dependency. The static ablation M0 uses only three features: dense relevance, query–candidate cosine and candidate length. Shared state descriptors are identical for all candidates in a state, cancel in the differences and get exactly zero coefficients, so the budget acts only through the feasibility filter, not the score.

Differencing cancels state-specific additive offsets, and the pairwise loss optimizes exactly the decision the allocator faces at each step. Unlike MMR's fixed λ, LMVU's weights are fixed at inference but act on geometry features that update with the selection, so the effective novelty penalty varies with what is covered: a candidate can rank high early and drop once its viewpoint enters the selection.

Allocation. Starting from an empty context, each step takes the argmax only among candidates whose full cost fits the remaining budget, adds it and updates the state, and stops when nothing fits; evidence is never truncated. Each step costs O(∣Ft​∣⋅18), maintained with incremental statistics and no pool-level similarity matrix. papers.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Zhiqiang Yuan, Shu-Dong Huang, Jiancheng Lv, Liwei Yang, Qiwei Yan, Kailin Lv, Jinchao Zhang
papers.abstract: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.
papers.summary: Embedding and generation are usually separate specialists with incompatible objectives; unified models like GritLM either switch attention regimes or train the two as parallel losses. ULME proposes predictive coupling so embedding and language modeling reinforce each other—aimed at RAG/agent pipelines that embed then generate the same query. ==Unifying embed+generate is about objective coupling, not shared weights plus a mode switch==.

deep_reading.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
deep_reading.content:
In RAG, in-context example selection and agent memory, the same query is usually processed twice: an embedder first encodes it into a vector for retrieval, and a generator then reads it again to answer. The two models are trained separately and their representations of the same query never interact. The authors, from WeChat AI at Tencent and Sichuan University, argue that a generative model, on its way to a coherent answer, already encodes an "answer-relevant reading of the query" in its hidden states, which is largely what a good embedding should be. They propose ULME, a post-training framework that inserts a chain of learnable slots into a causal decoder and uses a stop-gradient "predictive coupling" loss so that generation shapes the embedding. Across Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 at 8 scales from 0.5B to 8B, ==a single ULME checkpoint beats the strongest same-backbone open baseline on MTEB by 3.3–4.1 points==, while matching or beating a generation-only fine-tune on MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro and HumanEval.

## 1. The problem: existing "unified models" only unify parameters

Another line of work turns an LLM into a pure embedder: E5-Mistral and NV-Embed fine-tune causal LLMs contrastively and pool the last token, while LLM2Vec removes the causal mask to obtain a bidirectional encoder. They show decoder hidden states are enough for strong embeddings, but the fine-tuned model is no longer usable as a generator.

Putting retrieval and generation into one model is not new. GritLM trains one LLM with both a contrastive embedding loss and a language-modeling loss, and GEM injects embedding ability into a generative LLM through extra tokens and self-supervised contrast. The authors see these as only "partially unified", with two gaps.

**Mechanism.** GritLM switches to bidirectional attention for embedding and back to causal attention for generation, so its embedding readout and generative hidden states do not lie on the same causal trajectory.

**Objective.** The two losses are optimized in parallel over shared parameters but never supervise each other: generation does not depend on the learned embedding, and the embedding receives no direct signal from generation-side representations. Parameter sharing alone establishes no interface between them.

The concrete conflict is the readout position. Causal LLM embedders normally pool the query's last token, but in a unified model that position must also predict the first answer token. The authors call this a **representational collision**: retrieval needs a sequence-level state that is globally comparable under inner product, language modeling needs a position-dependent state that supports the LM head, and one hidden state is asked to play both roles.

## 2. Method: a slot chain and three losses

![ULME overview: one causal decoder trains three objectives on a shared chain of learnable slots: semantic contrast, answer generation, and stop-gradient predictive coupling.](figs/2610.30705/hf1.png)

**Slot chain.** Following latent chain-of-thought ideas such as Coconut and pause tokens, ULME inserts $N$ learnable slots between query $q$ and answer $a$, so a training example reads $q\,\|\,\langle\textsc{emb}\rangle_{1:N}\,\|\,a$ and a document is encoded as $d\,\|\,\langle\textsc{emb}\rangle$. The slots are ordinary positions in the causal forward pass: each attends back to the query and earlier slots, and every answer token attends to all slots. No mask is changed and no side branch is added; attention is causal throughout, and one forward pass yields both embedding and answer. Slot 0 is the **semantic embedding** and slot $N-1$ the **reasoning embedding**.

**Semantic retrieval loss.** A symmetric InfoNCE between the slot-0 query representation and the document representation, with temperature $\tau$ and cross-rank in-batch negatives.

**Answer generation loss.** Standard next-token cross-entropy over the answer span only; slots carry no token loss, but because the slot chain sits on the causal path that produces the answer, the language-modeling gradient reaches them through the answer's attention.

The authors note that these two losses alone are the "parallel objectives" of prior unified models: the semantic loss pins slot 0 to document space but says nothing about the answer, and the generation loss conditions on the slots but never asks any slot to represent anything specific.

**Predictive coupling.** The third loss aligns the query-side terminal slot $h_q^{(N-1)}$ with a pooled summary $r_{qa}$ of the answer-side hidden states from the same forward pass (by default their mean), via a one-sided in-batch InfoNCE with stop-gradient ${\rm sg}(\cdot)$ on the answer side:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}=-\log\frac{\exp(\langle h_q^{(N-1)},{\rm sg}(r_{qa})\rangle/\tau)}{\sum_k\exp(\langle h_q^{(N-1)},{\rm sg}(r_{qa,k})\rangle/\tau)}$$

The stop-gradient is deliberate: $r_{qa}$ sees both $q$ and $a$ and is more informed than $h_q^{(N-1)}$, which sees only the query and slots, so a well-posed objective lets the less-informed side reach toward the more-informed one; letting gradient flow into $r_{qa}$ would push the answer side toward whatever is easy to contrast in a batch, distorting the hidden states the generation loss must supervise. It amounts to one-sided distillation from the answer-side representation into a query-only latent available at inference. The total loss is a weighted sum with $\lambda_{\text{sem}}=\lambda_{\text{gen}}=1.0$, $\lambda_{\text{pred}}=0.3$, and defaults $N=4$, $\tau=0.05$.

**Illustration**: for the query "how do I deduplicate a Python list while keeping order", the training answer is code using `dict.fromkeys` plus an explanation. The semantic loss pulls slot 0 toward the matching document's embedding; predictive coupling pulls slot 3 toward the mean of that answer's hidden states. At inference no answer is generated: running the query plus 4 slots reads out the embedding.

## 3. Embedding results

Training uses LLM2Vec-format E5 contrastive data (embedding side) and OpenThoughts-114k (generation side), AdamW at $1\times10^{-5}$. Every number comes from the final checkpoint of a single run per configuration, with no capability toggled off and no head fine-tuned in isolation. Baseline numbers are those reported by LLM2VEC-GEN on the same backbone.

**MTEB(eng, v2) average:**

| Backbone | LLM2Vec | LLM2VEC-GEN | ULME |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 54.8 | 58.6 | 61.9 |
| Qwen3-4B | 56.8 | 60.6 | 64.1 |
| Qwen3-8B | 56.8 | 61.9 | 66.0 |

On Qwen3-8B ULME reaches 66.0, 9.2 points above LLM2Vec and 4.1 above LLM2VEC-GEN; gains over LLM2Vec are +7.1, +7.3, +9.2 across the three scales, and over LLM2VEC-GEN +3.3, +3.5, +4.1. On 8B against LLM2Vec, Retrieval gains +9.6, PairClassification +9.0, Summarization +9.0, STS +9.6 and Clustering +9.4. The authors note the largest lifts, Retrieval and Summarization, are on tasks whose target is itself a produced text. Against LLM2VEC-GEN, though, Clustering and Classification are slightly lower at 1.7B and 4B (−1.5, −0.6), and Classification is 0.5 lower at 8B, so the gain is not everywhere. By category, ULME's edge over LLM2VEC-GEN comes mainly from Retrieval (+8.2 to +8.9), Summarization (+7.0 to +8.6) and PairClassification (+5.3 to +5.7), with Reranking and STS gaining 1.5–2.5 points.

**Reasoning-intensive retrieval.** On BRIGHT (nDCG@10) ULME is 0.7, 0.8 and 1.2 points above LLM2VEC-GEN (1.7B/4B/8B), reaching 21.4 at 8B; on AdvBench-IR (lower is better) it cuts the score relative to LLM2Vec by 25.3% at 1.7B and 20.3% at 8B, another 1.3–1.8 points below LLM2VEC-GEN. Both directions improving rules out trading one property for another.

## 4. Generation results

Against a generation-only fine-tune (Gen-only FT) on the same OpenThoughts-114k data: on knowledge and math (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), ULME matches or exceeds it everywhere except a −0.1 on Qwen3-8B MMLU, with MMLU-Pro gains of +1.0, +2.0, +1.7 and GSM8K at 8B of 89.5 vs 78.6, 10.8 points higher. On code it is ahead at every scale, by 2.4–4.9 points on HumanEval and 3.0–4.9 on HumanEval+, with 67.7 vs 62.8 on HumanEval+ at 8B. The authors' explanation is that making the query slot summarize what the model will generate is especially informative for structured, functionally verified outputs. Both ULME and Gen-only FT sometimes trail the original backbone, which the authors attribute to distribution shift from continued training on OpenThoughts-114k rather than to the joint objective.

## 5. Ablations: the three losses really interlock

Ablations use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with the 10-task MTEB-lite for embedding and MMLU and GSM8K for generation.

**Number of slots.** With no slots ($N=0$, pooling the query's last token) MTEB-lite is 58.6, 5.2 points below the 63.8 of $N=4$, and MMLU is 2.0 lower, confirming the readout collision is a real cost. One slot recovers most of the gap, $N=4$ is best, and $N=8$ dips slightly, which the authors attribute to a longer chain diluting gradient per slot.

**Loss decomposition.** Removing the semantic loss collapses MTEB-lite from 63.8 to 31.2 with generation untouched; removing the generation loss drops MMLU by 14.7 and GSM8K by 15.8, while embedding falls only to 61.0. More telling are cases where a score moves although its own loss is untouched: without the generation loss embedding still loses 2.8 points, showing that answer-side states shaped by language modeling feed signal to the query slot; without predictive coupling generation is flat but embedding loses 3.6 points, the cleanest measure of what the coupling contributes, i.e. the cost of reverting to the "parallel losses" regime.

**Predictive target.** Mean pooling over the answer scores 63.8, a length-weighted mean 62.7, and the last answer token 61.9. The last answer token is also pulled by next-token prediction, so using it as the target imports local generation pressure. Generation barely changes under any choice, showing the two capabilities are supervised through distinct channels of the shared computation.

![Per-task gap between the semantic slot (slot 0) and the reasoning slot (slot N−1) on the 41 MTEB(eng, v2) tasks; positive favors slot 0, mean gap +0.65.](figs/2610.30705/hf2.png)

**The two slots do different jobs.** Slot 0 leads most on tasks where relevance is mostly lexical or entity overlap (SprintDup +4.84, CQAGaming +3.09, Touche2020 +2.85, HotpotQA +2.60); slot $N-1$ leads most where one must understand what a document claims, summarizes or expresses (ClimateFEVER +3.60, SummEval +2.29, StackExchangeP2P +1.83).

## 6. Limitations and industry relevance

The paper has no dedicated limitations section; the following are read from the setup. The main tables show only three Qwen3 scales, with the other five backbones in the supplement; all ablations use one backbone (Qwen2.5-7B) and a 10-task subset; each configuration is a single run with no variance reported; baseline numbers are cited from LLM2VEC-GEN rather than reproduced, and backbones it does not report are omitted; unified models such as GritLM and GEM are not compared in the same table; and neither the inference overhead of the slots nor end-to-end gains in a real RAG or agent system are reported.

For industry, the significance is the deployment shape. RAG and agent-memory systems commonly run an embedder and a generator side by side, each with its own memory footprint and maintenance. ULME offers a workable path: ==one checkpoint, causal attention throughout, no mode switching==, with neither embedding nor generation behind dedicated models, and embedding needs only the query plus 4 slots, not a generated answer. Two engineering details are worth borrowing: give the embedding readout its own positions instead of overloading the next-token position, and use stop-gradient to distil the side that "knows the answer" into a query representation usable at inference. Whether it really removes a separate embedding service depends on recall on your own corpus and the latency the slots add.

The stop-gradient is deliberate: rqa​ sees both q and a and is more informed than hq(N−1)​, which sees only the query and slots, so a well-posed objective lets the less-informed side reach toward the more-informed one; letting gradient flow into rqa​ would push the answer side toward whatever is easy to contrast in a batch, distorting the hidden states the generation loss must supervise. It amounts to one-sided distillation from the answer-side representation into a query-only latent available at inference. The total loss is a weighted sum with λsem​=λgen​=1.0, λpred​=0.3, and defaults $N=4$, τ=0.05.

Illustration: for the query "how do I deduplicate a Python list while keeping order", the training answer is code using dict.fromkeys plus an explanation. The semantic loss pulls slot 0 toward the matching document's embedding; predictive coupling pulls slot 3 toward the mean of that answer's hidden states. At inference no answer is generated: running the query plus 4 slots reads out the embedding.

3. Embedding results

Training uses LLM2Vec-format E5 contrastive data (embedding side) and OpenThoughts-114k (generation side), AdamW at 1×10−5. Every number comes from the final checkpoint of a single run per configuration, with no capability toggled off and no head fine-tuned in isolation. Baseline numbers are those reported by LLM2VEC-GEN on the same backbone.

MTEB(eng, v2) average:

BackboneLLM2VecLLM2VEC-GENULME
Qwen3-1.7B54.858.661.9
Qwen3-4B56.860.664.1
Qwen3-8B56.861.966.0

On Qwen3-8B ULME reaches 66.0, 9.2 points above LLM2Vec and 4.1 above LLM2VEC-GEN; gains over LLM2Vec are +7.1, +7.3, +9.2 across the three scales, and over LLM2VEC-GEN +3.3, +3.5, +4.1. On 8B against LLM2Vec, Retrieval gains +9.6, PairClassification +9.0, Summarization +9.0, STS +9.6 and Clustering +9.4. The authors note the largest lifts, Retrieval and Summarization, are on tasks whose target is itself a produced text. Against LLM2VEC-GEN, though, Clustering and Classification are slightly lower at 1.7B and 4B (−1.5, −0.6), and Classification is 0.5 lower at 8B, so the gain is not everywhere. By category, ULME's edge over LLM2VEC-GEN comes mainly from Retrieval (+8.2 to +8.9), Summarization (+7.0 to +8.6) and PairClassification (+5.3 to +5.7), with Reranking and STS gaining 1.5–2.5 points.

Reasoning-intensive retrieval. On BRIGHT (nDCG@10) ULME is 0.7, 0.8 and 1.2 points above LLM2VEC-GEN (1.7B/4B/8B), reaching 21.4 at 8B; on AdvBench-IR (lower is better) it cuts the score relative to LLM2Vec by 25.3% at 1.7B and 20.3% at 8B, another 1.3–1.8 points below LLM2VEC-GEN. Both directions improving rules out trading one property for another.

4. Generation results

Against a generation-only fine-tune (Gen-only FT) on the same OpenThoughts-114k data: on knowledge and math (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), ULME matches or exceeds it everywhere except a −0.1 on Qwen3-8B MMLU, with MMLU-Pro gains of +1.0, +2.0, +1.7 and GSM8K at 8B of 89.5 vs 78.6, 10.8 points higher. On code it is ahead at every scale, by 2.4–4.9 points on HumanEval and 3.0–4.9 on HumanEval+, with 67.7 vs 62.8 on HumanEval+ at 8B. The authors' explanation is that making the query slot summarize what the model will generate is especially informative for structured, functionally verified outputs. Both ULME and Gen-only FT sometimes trail the original backbone, which the authors attribute to distribution shift from continued training on OpenThoughts-114k rather than to the joint objective.

5. Ablations: the three losses really interlock

Ablations use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, with the 10-task MTEB-lite for embedding and MMLU and GSM8K for generation.

Number of slots. With no slots ($N=0$, pooling the query's last token) MTEB-lite is 58.6, 5.2 points below the 63.8 of $N=4$, and MMLU is 2.0 lower, confirming the readout collision is a real cost. One slot recovers most of the gap, $N=4$ is best, and $N=8$ dips slightly, which the authors attribute to a longer chain diluting gradient per slot.

Loss decomposition. Removing the semantic loss collapses MTEB-lite from 63.8 to 31.2 with generation untouched; removing the generation loss drops MMLU by 14.7 and GSM8K by 15.8, while embedding falls only to 61.0. More telling are cases where a score moves although its own loss is untouched: without the generation loss embedding still loses 2.8 points, showing that answer-side states shaped by language modeling feed signal to the query slot; without predictive coupling generation is flat but embedding loses 3.6 points, the cleanest measure of what the coupling contributes, i.e. the cost of reverting to the "parallel losses" regime.

Predictive target. Mean pooling over the answer scores 63.8, a length-weighted mean 62.7, and the last answer token 61.9. The last answer token is also pulled by next-token prediction, so using it as the target imports local generation pressure. Generation barely changes under any choice, showing the two capabilities are supervised through distinct channels of the shared computation.

The two slots do different jobs. Slot 0 leads most on tasks where relevance is mostly lexical or entity overlap (SprintDup +4.84, CQAGaming +3.09, Touche2020 +2.85, HotpotQA +2.60); slot $N-1$ leads most where one must understand what a document claims, summarizes or expresses (ClimateFEVER +3.60, SummEval +2.29, StackExchangeP2P +1.83).

6. Limitations and industry relevance

The paper has no dedicated limitations section; the following are read from the setup. The main tables show only three Qwen3 scales, with the other five backbones in the supplement; all ablations use one backbone (Qwen2.5-7B) and a 10-task subset; each configuration is a single run with no variance reported; baseline numbers are cited from LLM2VEC-GEN rather than reproduced, and backbones it does not report are omitted; unified models such as GritLM and GEM are not compared in the same table; and neither the inference overhead of the slots nor end-to-end gains in a real RAG or agent system are reported.

For industry, the significance is the deployment shape. RAG and agent-memory systems commonly run an embedder and a generator side by side, each with its own memory footprint and maintenance. ULME offers a workable path: one checkpoint, causal attention throughout, no mode switching, with neither embedding nor generation behind dedicated models, and embedding needs only the query plus 4 slots, not a generated answer. Two engineering details are worth borrowing: give the embedding readout its own positions instead of overloading the next-token position, and use stop-gradient to distil the side that "knows the answer" into a query representation usable at inference. Whether it really removes a separate embedding service depends on recall on your own corpus and the latency the slots add.

papers.title: Rubric-Calibrated Preferences: Cross-Query Calibration of LLM Judgments via Item Response Theory
papers.abstract: Rerankers decide which documents users and LLMs see, yet their standard metric, nDCG, relies on human relevance labels that are costly, sparse, noisy, and discretely graded. As rerankers approach each other in quality, nDCG on these labels therefore increasingly fails to separate them. LLM judges could supply dense labels. Relative judgments within one query tell even close candidates apart, yet their scores share no scale across queries. Absolute grades share one scale but are too coarse to distinguish documents of similar relevance. We propose Rubric-Calibrated Preferences (RCP), which combine both kinds of judgment. A listwise Bradley-Terry tournament orders each query's documents, and a rubric of yes/no criteria of increasing stringency provides an absolute standard. Item Response Theory (IRT), which scores test-takers based on their answers to common questions, then uses the shared criteria to put all queries' tournament scores on one scale. RCP's retrieval metric, RCP-nDCG, replaces nDCG's discrete labels with the resulting calibrated relevance probabilities. Against blind grades from 46 external annotators, calibration raises the correlation between a query's mean score and its mean human grade from 0.538 to 0.795. The probabilities rank a useful document above a non-useful one with probability 0.910 (AUC, chance 0.5), versus 0.651 for the benchmark labels. When the annotators' grades prefer one of two rerankers and exactly one metric agrees, that metric is RCP-nDCG in 72.4% of 185 comparisons (chance about 53%). On TREC-DL, RCP-nDCG sides with NIST assessors' grades on every reranker pair that these grades separate significantly. RCP-nDCG also resolves many of nDCG's ties and separates 1.9 times as many reranker pairs on NanoBEIR. Rubric calibration thus turns relative LLM judgments into dense relevance labels that are comparable across queries and agree with human judgment.
papers.summary: As rerankers cluster in quality, nDCG on sparse discrete human labels stops separating them. LLM relative judgments split close docs but share no scale across queries; absolute grades share a scale but are too coarse. Cohere’s Rubric-Calibrated Preferences (RCP) uses IRT for cross-query calibration; RCP-nDCG replaces discrete labels: useful-vs-not AUC 0.910 (vs 0.651 for benchmark labels); among 185 comparisons where only one metric agrees, RCP-nDCG is that metric 72.4% of the time; on TREC-DL it sides with NIST grades whenever they separate. nDCG failure modes hit 45.6% of NanoBEIR and 30.7% of BRIGHT queries. ==Reranker eval must move from discrete nDCG to dense, cross-query-calibrated judgments==.

deep_reading.title: Rubric-Calibrated Preferences: Cross-Query Calibration of LLM Judgments via Item Response Theory
deep_reading.content:
Across the 14 rerankers the authors evaluate, 45.6% of NanoBEIR queries and 30.7% of BRIGHT queries show one of nDCG's three failure modes: every reranker scores 1 (saturation), every reranker scores 0 (floor), or half or more of the pairs tie (compression). The root cause is that human relevance labels (qrels) are costly, sparse, noisy and discretely graded, and the problem worsens as rerankers converge. The Cohere authors propose RCP (Rubric-Calibrated Preferences): a listwise LLM tournament orders documents finely within each query, and a rubric of five yes/no criteria, via Item Response Theory (IRT), puts all queries on one ruler, yielding RCP-nDCG with continuous gains. Against blind grades from 46 external annotators, ==RCP gains rank a useful document above a non-useful one with probability 0.910, versus 0.651 for the qrels==; on NanoBEIR the share of reranker pairs separated significantly rises from 34.1% to 63.5%.

![On three queries, nDCG@10 saturates, floors or compresses 14 rerankers, while RCP-nDCG@10 spreads them.](figs/2609.35739/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: relative judgments share no scale, absolute ones are too coarse

LLM relevance judges can label at scale with quality close to human assessors, but both kinds of judgment have a weakness. **Relative judgments** (pairwise or listwise comparisons) separate close documents within a query, but scores from different queries share no scale, ruling out graded labels, shared thresholds and cross-query statistics. In Bradley–Terry (BT) terms, scores within a comparison set are identified only up to an additive constant, so different queries' scores are not comparable, and their spread differs when a judge is more decisive on some queries. **Absolute judgments** (grades) compare across queries, but the grades are coarse and leave many documents of a query tied.

The research question is whether a fixed set of yes/no criteria can put within-query LLM preferences on a scale shared across queries, with results that agree with human judgment. The authors test it in reranking evaluation, where independent human references exist and such scores could replace sparse, discrete, noisy qrels.

## 2. Method: the tournament sets the order, the rubric sets the scale

![RCP pipeline: Stage A scores each query's documents with a listwise Bradley–Terry tournament, Stage B records answers to five yes/no criteria, and IRT calibration puts all queries on one scale, giving RCP-nDCG's continuous gains.](figs/2609.35739/hf2.png)

IRT comes from testing: from test-takers' answers to shared questions, it places everyone on one ability scale. RCP's analogy is that **documents are the test-takers and rubric criteria are the questions**.

**Stage A: listwise BT tournament.** For each query's candidate set, listwise LLM reranking is repeated over windows of 10 documents, and the judge gives each document a score in $[-5,+5]$, which the prompt describes as a logit scale. Only the within-window soft preferences $p_{ii'}=\sigma(s_i-s_{i'})$ are kept, and BT scores are fit to them. A three-phase window schedule focuses comparisons on uncertain ranks and keeps mid-ranked documents away from dominant ones, which would depress their scores.

**Stage B: pointwise criterion evaluation.** The judge again reads 10 documents at a time but rates each on its own against an absolute standard, answering five yes/no questions of increasing difficulty:

| ID | Criterion | Diagnostic question | Discrimination γ | Difficulty β |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| C1 | Topical relevance | Is its topic clearly related to the query's information need? | 1.17 | −2.57 |
| C2 | Information utility | Does it contain specific, useful information to address the query? | 1.05 | −2.00 |
| C3 | Entity/detail match | Does it name and discuss the particular entity or detail in the query? | 0.94 | −0.25 |
| C4 | Direct answer | Does it explicitly and directly answer the query's primary question? | 1.16 | 0.71 |
| C5 | Thorough treatment | Does it treat the topic in depth rather than superficially? | 0.69 | 4.12 |

(Parameters are the NanoBEIR fit with judge Qwen3.5-397B.)

**IRT calibration.** BT scores and the abilities of IRT's two-parameter logistic (2PL) model both live on logit scales, so BT scores are mapped affinely to abilities:

$$P(Y_{ijc}=1)=\sigma\big(\gamma_c(\tau_j\hat\theta_i^{\rm BT}+\alpha_j-\beta_c)\big)$$

Each criterion's discrimination $\gamma_c$ and difficulty $\beta_c$ are shared across queries; each query has its own offset $\alpha_j$ (fixing BT's free additive constant) and scale $\tau_j>0$ (so that one logit of ability means the same relevance difference on every query). $\alpha_j$ and $\tau_j$ are estimated from that query's Stage B answers with BT scores held fixed, and the remaining parameters are fit by maximum a posteriori with weak priors. The calibrated ability is $\tilde\theta_{ij}=\tau_j\hat\theta_i^{\rm BT}+\alpha_j$. Since $\tau_j>0$, **the within-query order always equals Stage A's** (Proposition 3.1); calibration only changes how documents of different queries compare.

**RCP-nDCG.** nDCG's discrete gains are replaced by discrimination-weighted criterion pass probabilities:

$$g(\tilde\theta)=\frac{\sum_c\gamma_c\,\sigma(\gamma_c(\tilde\theta-\beta_c))}{\sum_c\gamma_c}$$

$g$ rises smoothly from 0 to 1, fastest where the rubric measures most precisely, with slope proportional to the rubric's Fisher information. The ideal ranking is the Stage A order. On NanoBEIR, $g$ is 0.22 at C1's difficulty and 0.69 at C4's; 79.3% of pool documents lie below C1's difficulty, 15.6% in between, and 5.1% above C4's.

**Illustration**: for the query "can aspirin prevent stroke", two documents differ only slightly in Stage A, but both pass C1–C3; on another query, the top document passes only C1. On BT scores alone the two queries' top documents look equally "relevant"; after calibration, the former is placed at a higher ability and earns a higher gain.

## 3. Setup and calibration quality

**Data and pools.** 13 NanoBEIR datasets (649 queries) and 12 BRIGHT tasks (1,366 queries), both with binary qrels; TREC-DL 2019 and 2020 (43 and 54 queries, graded 0–3 by NIST assessors); and the 8 corpora of ViDoRe v3 (2,419 questions, three-point grades). Each query's top-150 candidates come from Reciprocal Rank Fusion of Cohere Embed v4, Octen-Embedding-8B and BM25; positives the retrievers miss replace the lowest-ranked candidates, isolating reranking from first-stage recall. The 14 rerankers come from six families: Cohere, Contextual AI, Qwen3 Embedding, Voyage AI, Jina AI and ZeroEntropy. The primary judge is Qwen3.5-397B (17B active), the second is gpt-oss-120b, and TREC-DL uses the smaller Qwen3.6-27B.

**Blind human study.** 46 paid external contractors, each with at least a BSc in the annotated subject. Each contest is a query plus two rerankers' top-five lists; annotators grade the union in random order without seeing list membership, qrels or scores. The analysis covers 311 contests on 292 queries, 7,080 grades and 2,268 documents, three annotators per contest.

**2PL fit.** Given the calibrated score, criterion answers correlate only weakly (mean absolute correlation 0.123, against 0.60 for raw answers), meeting IRT's independence assumption; criterion parameters fit on other datasets cut a held-out dataset's cross-entropy by 60.6% against per-criterion pass rates. The per-query scale $\tau_j$ varies about threefold between its 5th and 95th percentiles (0.86 to 2.72), so the scale term is needed.

**Calibration.** On the judge's own 486,750 answers, a BT sigmoid that ignores the query scale has ECE 0.371, while the 2PL has 0.017; against the 7,080 human grades the ECE is 0.054. The Spearman correlation between a query's mean score and its annotators' mean grade rises from 0.538 for raw BT to 0.795 after calibration. On TREC-DL, the cross-query correlation of calibrated scores with NIST grades is 0.649 and 0.595, reaching 84.4% and 80.2% of the attainable ceiling.

## 4. Main results: more discriminative, and correct

**Label quality.** Over the 2,268 human-graded documents, RCP gains rank a useful document (mean grade ≥2) above a non-useful one with probability 0.910, versus 0.651 for binary qrels, because about half such pairs share a qrel label. Annotators rate 27.8% of documents without a positive qrel as useful and 37.5% of those with one as not useful, so qrels disagree with people in both directions.

**Discrimination.** Measured as the share of the 91 reranker pairs a paired t-test separates: on NanoBEIR, 34.1% under qrel-nDCG@10 versus 63.5% under RCP-nDCG@10. RCP-nDCG also separates more on BRIGHT, ViDoRe v3 and both TREC-DL years, and the conclusion holds with gpt-oss-120b as judge. Count-nDCG, which uses the rubric without the tournament, separates about as many pairs, so the added separation comes mainly from the rubric; but three blind LLM judges from other families prefer RCP-nDCG's ideal top-10 over Count-nDCG's on 80.6–98.8% of queries, so the tournament handles finer differences.

**Agreement with people.** In the 185 contests where exactly one metric sides with the annotators, that metric is RCP-nDCG 72.4% of the time (chance about 53%, since qrel-nDCG ties more often). When RCP-nDCG's margin is 0.20 or more, the annotators' verdict matches it in 96.8% of contests, against 53.1% for qrel-nDCG at the same margin. On TREC-DL, NIST grades significantly separate only 14 pairs in 2019 and 37 in 2020; RCP-nDCG agrees with NIST on all of them while separating 60 and 70 pairs.

![14 rerankers on NanoBEIR under qrel-nDCG@10 (left) and RCP-nDCG@10 (right, judge Qwen3.5-397B), colored by model family.](figs/2609.35739/hf5.png)

**Rank changes and the bias concern.** The largest change is ZeroEntropy: under qrel-nDCG@10, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Contextual v2 6B lead with 74.7 and 74.5 and the three ZeroEntropy models trail (66.5–67.0); under RCP-nDCG@10, zerank-2 and zerank-1 rise from ranks 14 and 13 to 1 and 2 (87.2, 87.1). zerank trains on pairwise preferences of an LLM ensemble, so the metric could be rewarding a shared signal. The authors' test: in 66 contests where RCP-nDCG favors zerank and qrel-nDCG the other, human annotators using no LLM chose zerank 78.8% of the time; excluding zerank contests, RCP-nDCG's 72.4% agreement drops to 68.1%, still above chance.

## 5. How robust is the rubric

On TREC-DL the authors test the shipped rubric and 15 variants. No significantly separated reranker pair reverses unless the rubric ignores the query or puts all criteria at one end of the scale. RCP is thus not very sensitive to rubric wording, but the rubric must span difficulties from lenient to strict. The authors also note the five criteria target general-purpose retrieval, and other applications may need others.

## 6. Limitations and industry relevance

The authors' acknowledged limits: RCP gains and human grades value each document alone and ignore redundancy between documents (notably on multi-hop tasks like HotpotQA); both measure perceived relevance, not factual correctness; the human questions resemble the rubric by design; relevance is hard to judge consistently, and two annotators grade within one step of each other in only 77.8% of cases; LLM judges may share the evaluated rerankers' preferences, so models trained on RCP signal are best tested on other labels. There is also a conflict of interest to note: all authors were at Cohere, Cohere funded the annotation, and two of the 14 rerankers and one of the three first-stage retrievers are Cohere products.

For retrieval and RAG teams, the value is shifting evaluation from sparse human labels to labeling the candidate pool once with an LLM, then scoring any reranker at no further cost. The code, all judged scores and the 7,080 human grades are released, so once a pool is labeled, any model that reorders it can be scored without further judge calls. The authors recommend benchmarks report ==RCP-nDCG alongside qrel-nDCG== rather than replacing it. Two practical cautions: below a margin of 0.02, agreement with humans is only 47.2%, near chance, so treat such margins as ties; and if your own reranker is distilled from LLM preferences, keep a human-judged set for cross-checking.
